words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Á heiðinni voru göngur. Siggi og Ketill fóru þangað með fólkinu og fénu.
Nú var heiðin undir vikri. Þar var ekkert gras.
Á heiðinni var Lóusel, kot Jóns og Sólveigar. Siggi og Ketill sáu það og gengu inn.
Jón sagði: „Ég fer aldrei aftur þangað.“
Heiðin var enn þar, en Jón fór ekki þangað.
words_with_history.note_en: Heiði means “heath, high moorland”. Heiðinn, “heathen”, is a separate word in modern Icelandic. [?] The old connection between heath and heathen, in Norse as in English, is a traditional but debated etymology; no derivation is asserted here.

pronunciation_note.rule: In sá, sáu and sáuð keep á distinct from a. In fór, fórum and fóruð keep ó distinct from o. The -st in fékkst and sást belongs to the second-person singular past here. Read the consonants together; do not add an extra vowel.

grammar.note_en:
A strong verb forms its past with a change inside the stem rather than the dental suffix of a weak verb. The stem is the part before the ending. Ablaut is the traditional name for the vowel alternation: fara → fór, “go → went”, and sjá → sá, “see → saw”. Compare the weak past kallaði, “called”, horfði, “looked”, and keypti, “bought”: their past has a dental consonant, ð/d/t, even when the vowel also changes. Strong verbs do not add that weak-past suffix. Not every form has an obvious written vowel change: koma → kom, “come → came”, must also be learnt as a strong pair.

The first and third person singular (ég, “I”; hann/hún/það, “he/she/it”) have no added personal ending in this past. Ég fékk (s006) is “I received/got”; þú fékkst (s077), “you received/got”. The second person singular here ends in -st: fékkst and sást. This -st marks “you” in the past; it is not the middle voice taught later. Some strong verbs use -t, but no such second-person cell occurs here, so none is displayed or practised. Plural endings are -um with við, “we” (komum, bjuggum, fórum, grófum), -uð with þið, “you” plural (fóruð, sáuð), and -u with third-person plurals (fóru, komu, sáu, grófu). The stem vowel can differ between singular and plural: sat/sátu, “sat”. It can also remain the same: fór/fóru, “went”. The spelling of bjuggum includes a consonant change as well.

The narrative core is fór, “went”; kom, “came”; sá, “saw”; gekk, “walked/went”; tók, “took”; fékk, “got/received”; hét, “was called”; varð, “became”. The quotation Hér bjuggum við (s038), “We lived here”, corrects Siggi’s future-in-context present búið þið hér aftur (s041), “you will live here again”. Ketill’s single word Bjuggum (s042), “Lived”, refuses that future. Þú fékkst lambið (s077) means “You got the lamb”. Tröllið varð að steini (s136), “The troll turned to stone”, contains the supported chunk verða að steini; do not analyse it as obligation verða að plus an infinitive. Nú verður þú að steini (s135) is “Now you will turn to stone”: the present refers to the immediate future. Lambið þitt varð kind (s068) means “Your lamb has turned into a sheep”; it remains a simple Icelandic past, not a compound perfect.

Dictionary reference only: fara – fór – fórum, “go – went (singular) – went (we)”; koma – kom – komum, “come – came (singular) – came (we)”; ganga – gekk – gengum, “walk – walked (singular) – walked (we)”; taka – tók – tókum, “take – took (singular) – took (we)”. Gengum and tókum are reference forms, not cells read in this story or exercise answers. The story uses gengu, “they walked”, and tók, “took”. No participle, supine construction or compound tense is taught here. Learn encountered principal parts, rather than deriving every strong past from a single vowel rule; the ablaut classes come later.

The tables contain only attested cells, sometimes quoting a clause from a longer segment. Fólkið fór (s122), “The people went”, has grammatically singular fólk; the row is a singular form, despite an English plural translation. Við fórum að kotinu (s055) means “We went to the croft”; Fóruð þið alla leið? (s054), “Did you go all the way?”; Á hverjum morgni fóru Bjarni og Jón snemma út á túnið (s063), “Every morning Bjarni and Jón went out early onto the home field”. Einn dag kom maður frá prestinum með blað (s094) is “One day a man came from the priest with a newspaper”; Við komum hingað með tvo bagga og nokkrar kindur (s010), “We came here with two packs and some sheep”; konurnar komu með hrífur (s063), “the women came with rakes”. Ég sá hann (s047) is “I saw it” (the raven); Sást þú hrafninn? (s046), “Did you see the raven?”; Og hvað sáuð þið? (s056), “And what did you see?”; Um hádegi sáu þeir kotið (s031), “At noon they saw the croft”. Ég fékk ekkert gjafakorn (s006) means “I received no relief grain”. Jón sat hjá lampanum (s141) means “Jón sat by the lamp”; Um kvöldið sátu allir í baðstofunni á Hömrum (s001), “In the evening everyone sat in the baðstofa at Hamrar”.

Keep supported items whole: sem (s101/s117), “who/that”, joins a noun to more information about it; it is reading support, not a relative-clause exercise. Vildi vera (s120), “wanted to be”, is a supported past modal with an infinitive. Komdu (s072) is “come” to one addressee, without teaching the imperative system. Manst þú (s113) means “do you remember”; it is a present item, not a strong past. Tvo bagga (s010), “two packs”, þrjár kindur (s008), “three sheep”, and fyrir tvær fjölskyldur (s090), “for two families”, do not introduce numeral drills. Á hverjum morgni (s063), “every morning”, á hverju kvöldi (s066), “every evening”, and á hverjum jólum (s120), “every Christmas”, are intact time expressions. Í vetur (s079) looks back to last winter; in s070/s090/s091 it looks forward to the coming winter. Á nóttunni (s117) means “at night”.
